objective: Enterprise-scale threat management and threat intelligence integration
secondaryObjectives: Security monitoring and analytics for enterprise operations
Incident response leadership across complex, multi-team environments

sources.cite: CompTIA SecurityX CAS-005 (V5) exam page: domains Governance, risk, and compliance 20%, Security architecture 27%, Security engineering 31%, Security operations 22%
sources.note: Relevant text: Security architecture covers network architecture ('segmentation, microsegmentation, VPN, always-on VPN, and API integration'), Zero Trust ('defining subject-object relationships'), security boundaries ('asset identification, management, attestation, data perimeters, and secure zones') and deperimeterization ('SASE, SD-WAN, and software-defined networking'); Security operations covers incident response including root cause analysis. The page has no objective text on federation by name. Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11; the CAS-005 objectives PDF was not re-read here. The course's unit titles are the course's own wording. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's federation-token-forgery (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The organization, the systems, the data and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You lead security operations engineering at Corvel Energy, a fictional utility with three business units and their own SOC teams. The sector's information sharing center has published an advisory about a campaign against utilities' remote access gateways.
handover: The advisory: indicators (IP addresses, file hashes), behaviors (gateway logins at night followed by new admin accounts) and the gateway versions targeted.
Each business unit runs its own SIEM content.
howItWorks: The console shows the alert queue, the event log and each asset's status.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: one business unit never acts on the email; the attacker's new admin account there goes unnoticed.
Check-in 3: with the gateway logs gone, nobody can tell which internal systems the attacker reached.
Check-in 4: the published hostnames are used in a new phishing wave against the company within days.

effects.log: Check-in 2: the hunt finds a match.
Check-in 3: the sector asks for confirmations.

intelPrompt.title: Indicators or behaviors?
intelPrompt.context: Each business unit's SIEM is separate.

choices.label: Push the indicators into the shared threat intel platform for all three SIEMs, and write a behavior-based detection (night gateway login then new admin account) deployed enterprise-wide

effects.log: Indicators and a behavior detection are live in all three SIEMs.

choices.feedback: Indicators expire as infrastructure rotates; behaviors persist. Central distribution covers every unit.

choices.label: Block the listed IP addresses at the firewalls
choices.feedback: Useful for a week; the campaign rotates infrastructure.

choices.label: Forward the advisory by email to the three SOC teams
choices.feedback: Each team acts differently or not at all; nothing is detected centrally.

huntPrompt.title: The behavior matched
huntPrompt.context: Business unit B's gateway has an admin account created at 02:14 after a night login.

choices.label: Open an enterprise incident with one lead, have unit B preserve gateway logs and disable the account, and hunt for the same behavior in units A and C

effects.log: A coordinated incident runs across all units.

choices.feedback: Multi-team incidents need one lead and shared scope; the same campaign may be elsewhere.

choices.label: Let unit B handle it as their local incident
choices.feedback: Unit B can contain its gateway, but nobody checks A and C.

choices.label: Reimage the gateway immediately
choices.feedback: Reimaging first destroys the logs that show what the attacker did next.

sharePrompt.title: Share what you found?
sharePrompt.context: Your detection and the attacker's account name pattern would help other utilities.

choices.label: Share the behavior detection and new indicators, sanitized of company data, through the ISAC under its traffic light protocol, after legal review

effects.log: Sanitized findings go to the ISAC.

choices.feedback: Sharing back improves everyone's detection; sanitize and follow the sharing rules.

choices.label: Don't share: it's embarrassing
choices.feedback: Other utilities miss a detection that would help them.

choices.label: Post the full incident details, including internal hostnames, on a public blog
choices.feedback: Publishing internal details helps attackers and breaks the ISAC's sharing rules.

reflection.question: Write the response record: how the intelligence became detection, how the incident was run across units, and what you shared.

scoring.modelReasoning: Threat intelligence is integrated at enterprise scale by distributing indicators centrally and, more durably, turning observed behaviors into detections deployed everywhere. A match in one unit becomes one coordinated incident with evidence preserved and the hunt widened. Sharing sanitized findings back through trusted channels under their rules strengthens the whole sector.
